On the same day, Mr. Speaker, 250 mothers met in a hall in Montreal east and questioned the Prime Minister. Does the Prime Minister know that we use our family allowances to buy food and pay oil heating bills?
Mr. Speaker, the questions those mothers directed to the Prime Minister of Canada are-

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has set up a task force to review the unemployment insurance
system. Amazingly, the Chairman of this group will be paid $750 a day plus $125 per day in travelling expenses. This is absolutely mind-boggling. Here we have a commission headed by an individual whose daily income is more than what the average claimant receives in a month.
I know that the Minister of Employment and Immigration is in agreement with me on the insanity of it all. She said on March 21, 1983, when commenting on the Macdonald Commission:
People see the special quirks and privileges, the appointment of commissioners at $800 per day.
The Minister went on to say:
To much of the Canadian public, Parliament has become an extravagant irrelevance. It is a circus show acting out its own fantasy in a make-believe world where neither money nor morality seem very real any more.
The Minister was right then and she is right now.

subsubtopic: OPENING OF TYRRELL MUSEUM IN ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week Premier Peter Lougheed officially opened the $30 million Tyrrell Museum which is nestled in the hills of the canyon of the Red Deer just west of the growing City of Drumheller in the beautiful Province of Alberta. The buildings are located not far from the confluence of the Red Deer River and the Kneehill Creek where, in 1884, one of Canada's outstanding geologists, Dr. Joseph B. Tyrrell, found the almost perfect head of a gigantic carnivore. This skull will soon be in the museum which bears his name, thanks to the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Siddon) and the former Minister of Communications, the Hon. Marcel Masse.
As I entered the museum I saw in front of me a giant globe of the planet Earth indicating that beyond we would find the colour, variety and the successful adaptation of life to a great diversity of environments. All around me were bones from the graveyards of the ages. Proceeding through a dark passage we stood looking into a vast chasm when suddenly the lights came on and I stood in awesome, silent, speechless amazement. It was as if we had just been propelled into the Drumheller Valley as it was three million years ago-a tremendous gigantic work showing skeletons of every type of dinosaur that ever existed, standing in their natural habitat.
Words cannot describe the portrayal of the earth's crust, the beginnings of life from three million years ago up to the appearance of man in the valley. It is the greatest palaeontology museum in the world. I urge every Canadian to join the

September 27, 1985
hundreds from other lands to visit the Tyrrell Museum. Drum-heller Mayor Bill Doucette welcomes the world to the Valley of the Dinosaurs.

Mr. Speaker, since the end of the summer recess, Canadians have been watching their Parliamentarians and how they are using the House of Commons, the noblest institution in this country.
Mr. Speaker, those same Canadians believe it is high time some Parliamentarians stopped using their seat in the House merely to talk about scandals and frivolous subjects. Their comments are a waste of time, and Canadians in general think their Parliamentarians should be making a more serious effort to seek a positive solution to the economic problems facing this country, not by discrediting our banking institutions but by renewing confidence in them. Furthermore, promoting investment in Canada will create jobs for our fellow Canadians, and that is what this Government is trying to do.

subsubtopic: DESCHENES COMMISSION-OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED U.S.S.R. VISIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the many aspects of the Nazi system that revolted and disgusted Canadians was its system of justice. The concept of Nazi justice is in itself a contradiction in terms because there was no justice in Nazi Germany. Individuals were jailed and often executed without the slightest regard for the principles of natural justice.
One of the other regimes which has shown contempt on a massive scale for the concept of justice as we know it is the Soviet Union. The gulags, the mental hospitals, the KGB, and the long history of Soviet human rights abuses should provide us with enough examples of Soviet justice to make us distrust that system absolutely. Yet, Mr. Speaker, the Deschenes Commission of Inquiry on war criminals is now considering travelling to the Soviet Union to hear evidence as part of its investigation.
[DOT] (mo)
Every Member of this House wants to see us track down those responsible for committing atrocities during the war. We all feel that these individuals must be brought to justice. But if we are to uphold the standards of our system of justice then, justice must not only be done, it must also appear to be done. The use of Soviet evidence by the Deschenes Commission must
be rejected if we are to uphold our own standards. There is some powerful symbolism here. If we use Soviet evidence, are we not perilously close to adopting the same tactics as those we are seeking to prosecute?
I call on the Government to prohibit the Commission from travelling to the Soviet Union to gather evidence.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN IMPERIAL BANK OF COMMERCE-TREATMENT OF PUBLIC AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has become clear that the large banks expect the Canadian taxpayer to pay millions of dollars to bail them out for their investments in the Canadian Commercial Bank. How have these same banks treated Canadians? The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce is one example of how the gigantic corporations have treated ordinary Canadians shabbily. Have they dealt with farmers facing foreclosure with compassion? No. Have they treated mortgage holders fairly? No.
While the Bank of Canada rate continues to go down, the Commerce has increased mortgage rates. The Commerce has a similarly negative record in its labour relations. Workers at the Commerce, many of them lowly paid women, have not had a regular wage increase since 1981. The bank wants complete freedom to reduce the hours of work whenever it wishes. It also insists upon compulsory overtime.
The Commerce also wants contract language that will prevent workers from taking cases of discrimination to the Human Rights Commission and that will exempt Commerce workers from the provisions of the Canadian Labour Code dealing with technological change. The same bank made over $400 million in profits last year.
It is incumbent upon the Government to force banks to show compassion and concern for farmers, home owners, and their own employees, before blindly pouring money into these wealthy corporations.

Mr. Speaker, the economic news this morning was most pleasing. I took pride in our Government on finding that the bank rate in Canada has dropped to its lowest level in seven years, and is now at 9 per cent.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-REACTION OF OPPOSITION PARTIES
CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-REACTION OF OPPOSITION PARTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have great difficulty in understanding the negative reaction of the opposition Parties to the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) announcement yesterday that our Government is pursuing a new enhanced trade agreement with the United States. Would the Opposition have Canadians stand by and lose their jobs to hundreds of protectionist Bills currently before the U.S. Congress, threatening our lumber, agriculture, steel, and fisheries industries, just to name a few? Would the Opposition have the Government discard a hundred billion dollar trade agreement? That is what will happen if we do not enter trade negotiations with the United States.
Canada is the only industrialized nation without guaranteed access to a market of 100 million people or more. The Macdonald Royal Commission, a commission set up by a previous Liberal Government and headed by a previous Liberal Finance Minister, has strongly recommended that Canada give high priority to the negotiation of freer trade arrangements with the United States to secure market access.
In an effort to score political points the Liberal Opposition is ignoring the reality that our economic future and jobs for Canadians depend on these trade negotiations. It appears that its Members do not care about Canadian jobs. They cannot deal with anything which may be positive for Canada, but Canadians know that major steps must be taken to ensure a prosperous future. I congratulate the Prime Minister on this historic initiative.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think I responded very fully to my right hon. friend. continually said that jobs are the key issue with regard to negotiating a deal with the Americans on trade. Mr. Speaker, some of the regrettable countervail instances are initiated by the United States; some are initiated by Congressmen. If there is much too much protectionism, as I indicated yesterday, from their side or from ours, it is suicidal. It just builds and explodes against job creation for everyone.

We have all these matters which makes us different and make us sovereign. These are not under discussion. What is under discussion is a commercial transaction designed to facilitate the creation of jobs, and germane to that process and the reason for it is, of course, the elimination of the kinds of pernicious obstacles to which my friend quite properly refers.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Prime Minister. Yesterday he insisted that he should not be informed in advance of police investigations against Ministers because, as he said, his advance knowledge could create the possibility of impeding justice. Does the Prime Minister not see the danger of not knowing what is going on? For example, can he work with a Minister in ignorance of the fact that the Minister is being investigated for endangering the state, or even for something less serious which puts the Minister's job on the line and maybe puts him in a desperate situation? How can the Prime Minister refuse to accept information about investigations under way against Ministers?

Mr. Speaker, I was referring to a specific case. When the Commissioner of the RCMP and the Solicitor General visited with me, I asked that they follow the exact procedures that had applied to my predecessor in similar cases. I was assured that this was the

September 27, 1985

process, whereby in this case I was advised that indeed search warrants would be sought against a Minister, but that the exercise of those search warrants would begin the next morning. It was not germane to me to be aware of the identity, at least in their view and in my view as well, to avoid the slightest suggestion-and I think the Hon. Member will agree that some very tenuous and difficult suggestions are made on the floor of the House-that I might have been aware of any information which might have allowed me even to suggest the inhibition of that inquiry. I sought not to be informed, having received the assurance that, immediately upon the execution of those search warrants, the Clerk of the Council or myself would be advised. That, to me, is a proper relationship between the Prime Minister and the administration of justice as it affects his Ministers.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has not stated the past practice accurately, and I would ask him to look into it. Why did he agree yesterday with the Hon. Member for Durham-Northumberland that it would be totally improper for the Prime Minister to know the details of an investigation before charges are laid by the RCMP against any Hon. Member of the House? He agreed with that. It is wrong, and today I invite him to retract it.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose we could discuss this matter on a case by case basis. This was brought to my attention by the Solicitor General, a position previously occupied by my hon. friend, and by the Commissioner of the RCMP. It was a courtesy explanation given to me in advance of the execution of the document. I understand, and I received the assurance before they came to my house, that this was conventional and proper and that this had transpired in the past. The value judgment was made that it would be inappropriate in the circumstances and of no need in the circumstances for me. I was advised that it was not a case of anything other than that which has been reported.
It was not a matter involving the national security. It was a suggestion that there might be a possible charge under the Elections Act. It was also made very clear to me-and, as a lawyer, I did not have to be told-that indeed the search warrant might result in the complete exoneration of the individual involved. As a result, I thought that that arms length relationship with the police forces was proper and that my conduct was proper as well.

The House resumed from Thursday, September 26, consideration of the motion of Miss MacDonald that Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976, be read a second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to stand in my place for a second day to deal with the subject matter of immigration. I believe 1 have approximately ten minutes of my allotted time left. In that time I would like to be succinct and clear in terms of urging members of the Liberal Party and members of the New Democratic Party to support Bill C-55. I do this, first, in order that the Bill can move quickly to committee; second, in order that amendments can be brought forward to make it a better Bill; and, third, to see that it is returned to the House of Commons as quickly as possible in order that we can get on with changing the system.

September 27, 1985
Immigration Act, 1976
It is clear that of 25 million Canadians most could not care less about this particular piece of legislation. The majority of Canadians are not involved in situations involving sponsorship of potential immigrants. However, for those who are involved, and those numbers are substantial, this is a critical and important piece of legislation.
I mentioned yesterday that the standing committee has had over 40 hearings on this subject since the month of January. Mr. Speaker, I think you will find that there is unanimous agreement in the committee that immigration levels must be increased in this country. We must turn the previous trend around. I think there is unanimous agreement in the committee that the scientific evidence is clear cut. Increased immigration leads to increased jobs. Increased immigration does not cost Canadian jobs.
Throughout our history one of the strengths of this country has been the reality that we have invited people from other nations to join with us to build our economic strength, to build our communities, to build our social system. We have been on an unfortunate backward trend in the last few years, that of a reduction in immigration, and I think it is time that we reversed that trend. When this nation does what it has been doing over the last four or five years, we begin to say no to some people who could really benefit this country. On a common sense basis people understand that and when they get an answer which is a no then they appeal the answer. That is what we have created. Members of Parliament have allowed that to happen. That is why we have such an enormous backlog of cases that deserve an appeal hearing.
The basic thrust, the reason for being, of this particular piece of legislation which has been brought forward is to increase the resources for the Immigration Appeal Board so those people stuck in the system can have a hearing. Our courts have said it must be an oral hearing, so the time demands on the Board have increased and there needs to be increased manpower. We were not able to get unanimous agreement in the month of June to move this piece of legislation through, and it is 90 days later and we are now debating it in second reading in the House. What that has cost is 90 days of extra waiting time for those thousands of thousands of people and their relatives and their friends who are jammed up in that system. If we debate in this Chamber for another 30 days or 60 days or 90 days then we are dooming those thousands and thousands of people to a longer wait.
We must have an immigration system that is quick, that is fair, that is sensitive, that operates in the nation's best interests and the interests of people who would like to immigrate to this country. We must have an appeal system characterized by those dimensions as well, quick, fair and sensitive. This Bill C-55 is in that tradition. As I listened to Members opposite I was really disappointed to hear that members of the Liberal Party, as signalled by their critic yesterday, intend to continue to fight the Bill. I hope that that decision was reached because of a misunderstanding rather than the reality of the situation.
Can I suggest to the Liberal caucus that our concern is identical to their concern and to the concern of the New Democratic Party about refugees?
We have a problem in the present system in terms of the determination of refugee status. We have a backlog in that system; we have a backlog in the over-all appeal system that is a logical consequence of the first backlog. The system is unfair simply on the dimension of speed. We have people who are in limbo for five years and longer in the present system. I think what the Members opposite are trying to do is to delay this Bill in the belief that it will bring pressure upon the Government to do something about the refugee system. If one reads the speeches, if one listens, that seems to be the mentality. I wish that members of all Parties, and many of them, had been present last night when we talked to Amnesty International about the Plaut Report. Unfortunately there was not, for good reason, a member of the Liberal Party present. But when that transcript is read carefully I think we will begin to discover that the reason we have gone wrong historically in this country in dealing with the refugee situation-and we deal with it better than most if not all other nations in the world, but we are still not dealing with it well enough-is that we have been treating the refugee decision-making process as an immigration decision-making process, and it is not. It is a question of human rights. It is a human rights protection process. The committee is going to have Rabbi Plaut before it next Tuesday night and we will then explore that in even more depth with him, but what has to be done in this country is that we must make that separation in a clear-cut manner. The Board, or the process that we put in place to deal with refugees, will have immigration consequences. If the determination is that a person is or is not a refugee, that person will still have the rights of immigration law and other categories. But we must not confuse the two things in this debate about the Immigration Appeal Board. If we are going philosophically to move in the right direction in terms of refugees, and to say clearly that that is a human rights decision to be made by tribunals that are skilled and sensitive to those aspects, then we are going to reduce the number of appeals that come to the Immigration Appeal Board. We are going to reduce some of that backlog the minute we get a decent system in place that is based on the philosophy that it should be based upon.
Having done that, we still must have some kind of immigration appeal process and at the moment that is lodged in the Immigration Appeal Board, and the cases that are before it, the thousands and thousands of cases that are jammed up and waiting in line, are not all refugee cases. An enormous portion of those cases are landed immigrants or citizens of Canada who want to sponsor a relative, bring him or her to his country, and they feel they have been treated unjustly and they want to appeal. The longer the Opposition delays this Bill the more clearly they are sentencing all of those family members to a continued period of uncertainty and inquietude and psychological stress and turmoil.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I cannot say more strongly that the time to act is now. Today is the very best day to let this Bill

pass out of this House of Commons and into committee. Mr. Speaker, you have a sensitive committee, you have a hard working committee. It will revise the bad parts of this Bill and bring it back quickly. Let us get that part of the world cleared up so the committee members and the Government can concentrate on clearing up the refugee situation, because that is the next major piece of initiative that has to be dealt with. The Government is committed to it, your committee is committed to it and I hope all Members of this House of Commons are committed to that process as well. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much many of the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) and in particular his statement, and I think I have it almost word for word, that the reason we have gone wrong procedurally in our well meant attempt to handle the flow of refugees who apply from in Canada is that we have been treating refugee decision-making as an immigration process. As he says, it is not; it is a human rights process.
I was interrupted by a couple of Hon. Members on business relating to this debate and I was not clear enough on exactly what he said after that. It appears that the effect of this Bill, as explained by the Minister yesterday, may be to bring more of the refugee decision-making into the Immigration Appeal Board work. In other words, it would compound the problem the Hon. Member has just defined. When he says that we must make that separation a clear-cut matter, how does he deal with what the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. McLean) said yesterday and with what the Hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) said in her June 19 statement, that the increase in board staff will-this is the only reason she gave-enable us to tackle the refugee backlog? In other words, it seems that the Cabinet thinks of the IAB as the way to deal with this increase in refugee problems whereas the Hon. Member who spoke seems to say that that is the wrong course.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for the question. The concept of ministerial responsibility requires Ministers to administer the law as it sits. Today, at this moment, there is a refugee determination process and an appeal process through the IAB. Until the law is changed that process will continue.
I think it is clear that the Government will not be able to act on the Plaut Report before some time in November and maybe even December. It is clear that the committee is working hard to provide advice to the Government by the end of October so we can influence that decision. Members of the Government caucus and the Opposition may or may not agree with the decisions which are made. However, it is impossible at this point to know how long it will take to get this through because we do not know what it will say. In the meantime, life goes on. In the meantime, refugees are jammed up in the IAB process. They are entitled to that process under Canadian law and we are denying them access because we do not have enough staff to deal with it. In the interim, for the next three, four, five or
Immigration Act, 1976
six months, we cannot deal with all the cases but we can deal with a lot more if we move this Bill quickly through the House. We can then remove the uncertainty and psychological stress these people are suffering. However, at this point in time we must deal with the law as it exists and I think that is what the Minister is doing, administering the law as it exists.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member made a passing reference to four, five or six months. Does he wish to state whether it is his opinion that that would be enough time for the legislation to be completed? He spoke about the Government acting in November, which would be in two months. 1 do not know whether he means to initiate legislation or to bring it to completion. It makes a difference as to how we approach this problem. Are we dealing with something which could become a long-range band-aid to cover the refugee problem, or would it be a more short-range matter, particularly regarding the problem of sponsorship, particularly Canadian residents sponsoring their relatives? Is he suggesting that in six months we would have new legislation in place to handle the refugee problem?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows I am not a member of the Cabinet, but August was an important month in immigration matters because we had a clear-cut signal that the Government recognized the importance of this subject matter. We now have a Minister of State devoted to this matter on a priority basis. That Minister and the Minister of Employment and Immigration have clearly signalled that changes to the refugee process are a priority for the Government.
I believe that if the committee makes a unanimous set of reasonable recommendations by the end of October, that will facilitate the process. The Government, if it has the support of all three Parties, can move more quickly. If we do not have that support, then it takes time. Once we finish with it, the Senate has to deal with it. If the Liberals are opposed in the Senate, they can string it out forever. If not, then it can move forward quickly. These things are beyond the Government's control. However, I think it is crystal clear that the Minister, members of the committee and members of the caucus want us to move quickly and correctly to get the new legislation in place. But speed requires co-operation from both opposition Parties.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a small comment regarding refugees. The Hon. Member, who is chairman of the committee concerned, mentioned that the problem of refugees is an important one. I wonder whether we are going to move in the direction of defining exactly what a political refugee is. Up until now we have been dealing with all sorts of refugees from different countries, some of whom are not political refugees. I think there should be an exception made for political refugees and I hope the committee he chairs will act fast on that.

I thank the Hon. Member for the question. The Plaut Report and the committee are dealing with Cana-

September 27, 1985
Immigration Act, 1976
da's obligations under international law regarding the protection of and asylum for conventional refugees. These are people who, if they returned to their country, have a well-founded fear of persecution on the basis of political activity, race or religion. Those are three definite factors. Yes, your committee is struggling with a process which will enable them to determine in a sensitive way whether refugee claimants have that kind of a fear and whether it is well-founded. However, I think the situation requires some sensitivity in the decision-making process because the situation in a given country can change overnight. One day there is a coup and the next day a different Government is in place. One day a particular person had no legitimate and well-founded fear of persecution, but the next day, after the Government has changed, he does. That is why I know in advance that the committee will not be able to provide the kind of definition which will last us for all time. What we will be able to do, I hope, is to provide a system which is sensitive and up to date. Canada has a well-deserved reputation for providing protection and asylum to the persecuted. We want to maintain that reputation and improve it, and I am convinced that Members on the Government side are dedicated to doing just that.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am indeed pleased to be able to participate in this debate on Bill C-55. However, I must take issue with the initial remarks of my friend from Calgary West. At the beginning of his remarks today he said that the vast majority of Canadians could not care less about this Bill. I believe that the federal policy on immigration is very important with regard to human and social impacts. Most Canadians have an interest in immigration. In my constituency of York West, and in a large number of other constituencies, immigration is one of the most important problems next to unemployment. I would like to set the record straight and say that as far as our Party is concerned immigration is a very important aspect of federal public policy to most Canadians.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I do not necessarily disagree with all of the contents of this particular Bill. Clause 6 would be amended to accord permanent residents the right of appeal which is presently only available to Canadian citizens who sponsor applications for landing. The Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) says that members of the Opposition are opposing the Bill simply for the sake of opposition. That is not the case. We have some legitimate concerns with this Bill, although we also agree with certain clauses of it. The Member for Calgary West also says that we must not continue to waste time. We are not wasting time, Mr. Speaker. This Bill was only introduced in this Chamber yesterday and we have only had some hours of discussion on it. If the Government is concerned about wasting time, why did it not introduce this Bill a year ago? Members are laughing-that is their prerogative.
What will this Bill do for the plight of 20,000 to 23,000 refugees who are awaiting an answer on their future? I do not believe that this Bill does very much for them. With regard to the clause that will increase the number of commissioners on the Appeal Board from 18 to 50, an off-the-cuff reaction would be that it would speed up the appeal process. However, that is not the only approach that can be taken to speed up the procedure. That approach addresses the symptoms of the problem rather than the cause. Another approach that could be taken is to question, as did the Plaut Report, whether many of these individuals ought to be coming before the Appeal Board, whether they do not have the right to remain in this country rather than pleading their case before a board. That is a way of attacking the cause of the problem rather than the symptoms. With respect to increasing the number of commissioners, what will we do with the additional commissioners once we eliminate the backlog? This would establish a temporary structure rather than looking at the long-term issue. I would like to illustrate this thinking by a real life example.
There is a couple in my riding from Argentina who arrived in this country several years ago with refugee status. They fled Argentina because they were teachers there during the military regime. As you know, one of the first communities that was persecuted by that regime was the community of educational institutions. Their home was ransacked and burned and their child was kidnapped. They fled to this country and have been here for a number of years. They made sacrifices to learn English and now both speak it very well. They both hold down responsible jobs and are involved in the community at large as well as in the Latin American community. Their six year old daughter speaks nothing but English, having been involved in our educational system from the ground floor. These individuals have recently been asked to return to Argentina on the basis that there is now a civilian Government there.
Is that a fair request, Mr. Speaker? I think not. I am sure that if Members of the House met this couple they would come to the same conclusion based on two premises. The first is that if these people returned to Argentina the fear of persecution which they felt three years ago would still be there, albeit on a different level. They would fear also that the Government may revert to the previous military dictatorship. The second premise is that they have made a genuine effort to adapt to this country by learning the language and life style and establishing roots here. They are asking themselves whether it is fair to be asked to return to Argentina after making such an effort to become Canadian citizens.
I think this example highlights the problem with this Bill. This legislation assumes that the solution to the refugee problem is to increase the number of commissioners to hear appeals. The case that I just outlined, and I am sure hundreds, thousands of others, ought not to have to come before the Appeal Board at all. These people will be living in danger if they return to their place of origin. They have made sacrifices and contributions to this country and their problems should be looked at from a compassionate philosophical point of view.
September 27, 1985

I am concerned that the Government is not prepared to do that. In his speech yesterday the Member for Calgary West indicated that the Government has the progressive will to deal with immigration on a compassionate basis. I fear that that is not the truth because I have not seen any evidence of that compassion with respect to immigration. The Member said that he and the committee are in favour of raising immigration levels. However, within weeks of being sworn in last September, with no study or public consultation with professionals serving the immigrant community, the Government reduced the number of entrants to this country from 100,000 to 80,000. How can the Member now say that the Government is in favour of increasing the level after having reduced it? That does not show to me a progressive will with regard to immigration.
Let us also look at the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration, which has a majority of Conservative Members. One of the first things that committee did was to embark upon a path that would suggest that people entering this country should, in large part, be entrepreneurs. It should be made perfectly clear that it was a Liberal Government that established a system of applications for entrepreneurial immigrants. Not only do we welcome those who want to come to this country, we want to make specific provisions for those immigrants who could come here to invest and establish a shop or factory and provide positive economic spinoffs. However, unlike the Government today, our Party has never been prepared to make entrepreneurial ability the basic immigration requirement. I suggest that the committee which is made up of a majority of Conservative Members, is on dangerous ground if it wishes to pursue an immigration policy based purely on entrepreneurial ability, and I hope that the Minister does not decide to follow that course. Such a policy would deny one of the realities in this country that poor immigrants who came to this country with very little became wealthy. The Member from Alberta continues to laugh. Again, that is his prerogative.
It is also a fact that regardless of the economic status that the Government is seeking, many individuals came to Canada with only their trade and desire for betterment, but they have worked and helped to build this country. Many immigrants took jobs that many other Canadians did not want. They too contributed to this country. Our Party will not support a policy for increased immigration if it only applies to the rich.
It is very dangerous for the committee, led mainly by Conservatives, to embark on such a discussion. While we agree that we need entrepreneurs and investors to come to this country and open factories and stores to provide jobs for Canadians, we do not agree that the corner-stone of our immigration policy should be based on whether or not a potential immigrant is whealthy. This country was not built only by wealthy immigrants and it will not continue to grow only with wealthy immigrants. I question the Government's "progressive will" because I have not seen the evidence to put my fears to rest.
Immigration Act, 1976
Another matter not addressed in this Bill concerns the family assistance stream in our immigration policy. This area merits careful consideration because family reunification has been stressed as a priority for immigration in this country. I hope the committee will consider amendments to the Bill that will make the family assistance level stronger.
As I stated at the beginning of my remarks, many of my case files in York West deal with immigration. Many of those cases concern the fact that Canadians living here are frustrated at their inability to sponsor successfully relatives abroad who wish to come to Canada. Therefore, more latitude must be provided in that stream.
It is true that economics must be taken into consideration with immigration and that we must be careful not to augment unemployment in certain sectors of our economy. However, I agree with the Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) that there is no study indicating that increased levels of immigration coincide with an increased rate of unemployment.
The provisions under the family assistance level in immigration is cause for frustration by Canadians who want to sponsor relatives. However, unlike refugee applications, entrepreneurial applications and applications by those who do not have relatives here, the family assistance application would be most reassuring to those who have concerns about immigrants negatively affecting our country. A broader family assistance immigration policy would alleviate much of the concern of those who believe that increased immigration will cause other Canadians to suffer. An immigrant who is sponsored by an individual living in Canada can be protected if he or she falls on hard times.
There is a definite strength in the family unit in this country and therefore I believe that an immigrant who has relatives living in this country can be given that family support when he or she faces hard times. This is an area of immigration policy that should be given more attention by the House because it will soften those critics who believe that immigration should be based on economics.
I hope the Hon. Member, who is Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, will take my concerns seriously because in my first year as a Member of Parliament, the family assistance level in immigration has been one of my priorities in the riding of York West. I know from my discussions about this problem with other Members that it is an issue in their constituencies as well. Therefore, the House should take notice that it must seriously review that family assistance policy in immigration.
Mr. Speaker, I indicated that I agree with certain parts of the Bill. I am riding today because I feel passionately about immigration and matters affecting my constituents and prospective Canadians who want to determine their future. This Bill will not solve the bottleneck referred to by another Hon. Member in reference to those 23,000 individuals who are waiting to hear about their future. Those who are waiting in groups of 10 or 15 in hotels in Toronto and Montreal want answers. I believe that the Plaut Report provided the right answers and approach to the problem. We should be address-

ing the question of whether these individuals should present their case before the Appeal Board, as suggested in the Bill, or whether the Government should have the compassion, integrity and vision to consider these people as human beings who are prepared to sacrifice and become involved in the mainstream of Canadian life. I rise in my place to make that point. I also rise in my place to suggest to the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration that we in this Party will not and will never waste the time of the House on this Bill. We will certainly be taking him up on the offer to move amendments in order to strengthen the viability of this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, 1 listened carefully to the remarks of the Hon. Member oppsite, and would agree with most of them. This is not a panacea to solve the problem. It will simply make the world a little better for a few more people. They deserve our help, and that is the reason for speed.
Let me make another comment. The degree to which parliamentarians turn the subject of immigration to partisan political advantage, I think, confuses the Canadian public and makes a sane, sensible and humane immigration policy a little more difficult to achieve. One of the ways we do that, sometimes deliberately and sometimes inadvertently, is to take a point of view, take it out of context and put it into some other kind of point of view. The standing committee's second report dealt with levels. We could not get three Party agreement to it, partly because we misunderstood each other. The thrust of that report was the issue of using immigration policy, in part, to create jobs.
I do not think there is any disagreement in this House that someone who lives in Canada who cannot find a job experiences trouble. Those of us who have been aound for six years have seen-certainly someone from Calgary has seen-a situation where a shortage of employees turned into a surplus in a short period of time. Calgary went from a 3 per cent or 4 per cent unemployment rate to a rate 2 per cent higher than the national average for a year and a half. When you go into people's homes and find no food in the fridge and see discouragement on their faces, it is a tragedy.
When we bring refugees or immigrants of one kind or another to this country, they come with a sense of hope and optimism because this is the new life and a new opportunity. If our economy cannot support jobs for those people, then the disappointment is enormous.
There are 9,000 South Vietnamese refugees in the City of Calgary, many of whom are still having difficulty finding employment because the economy of Calgary crashed. Others have found employment.
It was the feeling of the committee that a small portion of increased immigration levels should be devoted deliberately to the kinds of immigrants who could create jobs for the refugees, for the assisted relatives and for those already here. If we want a kind of racial backlash-
What is your question?

-then let us continue with a shortage of jobs because then people look around and say, "He took my job. We do not want any more immigration". If we had a surplus of jobs and a shortage of employees, then the national will to increase immigration levels would be clear and consistent.
Standing in this House today in the year 1985, it is not clear and it is not consistent, partly because the economy is not in good shape. I think it behooves members of all Parties to say levels should be increased, partly for the sake of job creation. People need jobs. Immigrants need jobs. It is not a bad piece of public policy to reach out to other countries and bring those jobs and people to Canada. I hope we can get together on that.

Mr. Speaker, once again I draw the attention of the House to the Hon. Member's leading-off statements. He said that he hopes that Members do not turn and twist remarks around, but that is what he just did. He was trying to insinuate that this Member and this Party is somehow against creating jobs for Canadians or for immigrants. That is not the case. I am not prepared to labour that point.
He drew the example of a large number of refugees in his city who cannot find work. I have met with refugees in the City of Toronto who cannot find work either. Part of the problem is that everybody knows they are refugees. Various piece of documentation indicate they are refugees. Their social insurance numbers indicate they are refugees. As long as that unknown status is allowed to continue and fester, they will not have those jobs to which the Member alludes.
There are a number of jobs in our communities being created and made available to Canadians from various parts of the country. These individuals who have this refugee cloud over their heads have a secondary and tertiary problem simply because their status has not been resolved. In many cases, these individuals would be able to do the jobs that Canadian employers require, but they are held back simply because of their status.
The Hon. Member also mentioned about the problem of bringing in immigrants and increasing levels of immigration. We do that in many sectors of our economy. Take a look at the tool and dye makers, Mr. Speaker. We still go to Great Britain to get tool and dyemakers. I am not suggesting that a tool and dyemaker in Great Britain or a tool and dyemaker in Australia is a rich entrepreneur. That is an example I was drawing to the Hon. Member's attention. That committee of his was definitely looking at increasing levels of immigration based on the wealth of those individuals.
No. Read the report.

It is there for everybody to see. In the third report the tune was changed. The Minister never accepted the second report. Rightfully so because the second report was most regressive. The second report denied the existence of the Canadian reality up to today and would have denied it tomorrow as well. When I make those comments, I do not make them to misinterpret the Hon. Member's suggestion.

You do.

It is very clear in the report not only for these Members but for Canadians across the country to see. I challenge the Hon. Member to bring forward that second report and get approval in this House, regardless of the absolute majority and regardless of closure tactics.

speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock, the Chair was ready to recognize the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap).

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act as it relates to the Immigration Appeal Board. Although it is a small Bill in some ways, it has been rehashed and unfortunately it has not proceeded as fast as any
Immigration Act, 1976
of us, myself included, would have liked. I will deal with the reasons for this, and I have some suggestions about how 1 think we could do better.
First I should like to begin by laying very positive groundwork by accepting the principal statement made this morning by the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes). 1 have acquired great respect for his work as Chairman of the committee this year. I believe that he, along with others, will be able to work out some kind of negotiation on this matter. 1 know he has tried very hard. I do not have the "blues", but I wrote down as quickly as I could what he said this morning at the beginning of his remarks. He said that the reason that the Government, Parliament and the country of Canada have gone wrong with refugee work, despite our good intentions, is that we have been treating refugee determination as an immigration question and, as he said, it is not. It is a human rights question, and we must make that separation clear. Rabbi Plaut brought this to our attention in his report earlier this year, but I strongly agree with the way the Hon. Member for Calgary West stated it. On that basis, I believe we can get the Bill passed through all stages soon.
However, in his later remarks, the Hon. Member made some statements which were unintentionally misleading. He said that there had been 40 hearings since June on this subject, and that we were unanimous on increasing immigration levels and on immigration not being a threat to jobs. That is true, but it is not relevant to this debate. Almost all those 40 hearings had nothing to do with the refugee question. The biggest portion of them concerned the entrepreneurial program. We had very few meetings to deal with refugees and only one meeting, in the last week of Parliament, to deal with the Bill. That is very unfortunate.
Also the Hon. Member said that he regretted the 90 days of delay from the end of June to the end of September. Perhaps he has forgotten an earlier delay, that in November, 1984, the Minister asked for and received from the two opposition Parties unanimous support for increasing the Appeal Board to 30 or 35 members but did not act on it. From November to June there was a delay of much more than 90 days.
The Hon. Member who spoke yesterday on behalf of the Liberal Party neglected to mention that the previous Government, under his Minister of Employment and Immigration, obtained unanimous consent from the opposition Parties in February, 1984, but did not put it through. Neither Government was willing to use the unanimous agreement, either in February, 1984 or in November, 1984. I do not know the reason for this, but it is not becoming to either of the two Parties to sound injured now about delay.
When the Bill was brought in, it was almost at the last minute. There was practically no time to negotiate any amendments. It contained some surprises that were not in the original request to which we had agreed. We were able to do a little negotiating with the very strong help of the Chairman, but not enough to make it viable.
The particular problems were that the amendments of the Minister would have potentially hurt the case of every Canadi-

September 27, 1985
Immigration Act, 1976
an who was appealing on behalf of a relative he or she wished to sponsor. They had been turned down by the staff-and I will return to the staff because I believe it is the root of our problem-and appealed to the Immigration Appeal Board. Rather than a three-person panel to hear appeals, the Minister wanted to cut it down to one. Every lawyer with experience in this regard has indicated to me that that would be unjust. The Minister stated in her June 19 press release that it was to deal with the refugee backlog and would enable the Immigration Appeal Board to hold "a greater number of oral hearings for refugee claimants by increasing the size of the Board". Also she indicated that a requirement by the Supreme Court to have oral hearings has "made it necessary to expand the Immigration Appeal Board in order to cope with the extra work-load". In June, that was the only reason she gave for this legislation. It was therefore impossible to interpret it in any other way than the way she interpreted it, which was that this was a program to deal with the backlog of 13,000 or 14,000 refugee hearings and that this would mean she would confirm the principle that refugee determination is an immigration matter. That is the very principle that the Chairman of the committee and Rabbi Plaut's Report denies. This legislation would have tripled the size of the Board and reduced the quorum to one. Refugee hearings would have been run through the system like sausages through a sausage machine. That is the way the Plaut Report, the Chairman of the committee, Members of the House and members of the public who have worked with refugees unanimously agree is the wrong way to go.
We have found on experience that the Immigration Department, dominated by the concept of enforcement, is not the appropriate body to deal with people claiming refugee status. It is not only that the Department is hostile to refugees. The former Executive Director of the Department, as reported in the press, repeatedly called refugees queue jumpers and talked about how many of them are bank robbers, terrorists or even Irishmen. I am not quite sure what he had against Irishmen. He continually slandered refugee applicants and misrepresented the statistics. For example, he pointed out that only about 35 per cent of refugee claims were approved by the Minister. He did not point out that after the Refugee Status Advisory Committee had made its recommendations, he and other staff members added their further recommendations behind the scenes so that the Minister's decision was not based simply on the Refugee Status Advisory Committee but also on pressure from staff members.
As I have said, Department of Immigration staff members are enforcement minded and seem to think that they were appointed principally to keep people out of Canada. I agree with the Chairman of the committee who said that we need to have more people come to Canada, but we have to climb over our own staff members to get them here.
Staff members are also hostile to family reunification. In my office, which deals with a great deal of immigration business, there are at least four staff members who spend at least half of
their time dealing with immigration matters. We have noticed more and more delays in the applications for family reunification, particularly those coming from non-European countries. Files get lost. Letters do not get answered. Little nit-picky points are raised that were never raised in the past. It is as though someone were going over and over these applications looking for excuses to keep these people out.
I have a file with me relating to claims from Pakistan. It seems that our representatives in Pakistan must have pledged not to let anyone into Canada if they can possibly prevent them from coming. I have encountered many negative examples of this from Pakistan. For example, there is the case of a Canadian who wishes to bring his parents to Canada as well as his sister who is unmarried and of an age at which in Pakistan it would be considered socially improper to live alone. This matter has been going on for about two years. We cannot get a straight answer to our humanitarian plea. All we get is bureaucratic answers going by the book. I could tell the House of many more cases just like this one.
Department staff members are hostile in their actions toward people who are trying to enter Canada for family reunification reasons. The statistics reflect this. One of the things that has come to light lately is that the number of appeals coming before the Immigration Appeal Board has been rising. In 1981, there were 1,136 such appeals. In 1982, the total was 1,296; in 1983, it was 2,077; and in 1984, it was 2,376. Within those statistics, it can be shown that family class sponsorship appeals have almost doubled in three years from 642 to 1,203. Refugee determination has more than doubled from 297 to 669. Other cases including those of illegal immigrants who are being deported after having made their cases have risen from 197 to 504. That is more than double.
Why has there been this increase in appeals to the Immigration Appeal Board? It is because family reunification is being blocked in two ways. First there was a freeze put on family reunification on May 1, 1982 through the requirement that any assisted relative not be considered unless he or she has a certified job offer. By the Minister's own estimate at the time, that chopped family reunification by about 25 per cent of its previous volume. The other way it is blocked is through the actions of staff members. People cannot get their relatives into Canada, so they come here as illegals or as refugee claimants. Then, along with direct appeals on family reunification, these cases go to the Immigration Appeal Board. That has caused this crisis, more than a doubling of the total number of cases before the Board in three years.
In spite of all that has been said about family reunification, the actual practice of the previous Government as well as of the present Government has been to reduce immigration. In 1981, immigration levels fell short of the Department's planned levels by at least 1,500. In 1982, the level fell short by
9,000	and in 1983, the year in which we felt the full effect of the 1982 freeze, it fell short by 45,000. In 1984, it fell short by almost 2,400. These people were shut out by our bureaucracies, our overseas offices and, to some extent, our Canadian offices as well. The principal problem is the attitude of those
September 27, 1985

working in our overseas offices. I met members of the overseas staff this summer and you have to meet them to believe their attitude on immigration, Mr. Speaker. It is really something else.
We have been cutting back on immigration, not because of a decision made by Parliament but because of staff practices. Therefore, we are hearing more appeals through other channels, whether legitimate or not. The attitude of members of the enforcement section of the Immigration Department is such that they try to keep people out of Canada. This has caused an increase in illegal immigration and in appeals before the Immigration Appeal Board.
Granted, we do need a short-term solution. Even if we could follow the advice of Rabbi Plaut and the Chairman of the Immigration Board by separating refugees entirely from the immigraton process until a claim has been determined, we would still have to deal with the backlog that exists. However, people who have worked hard as volunteers to help immigrants and other refugees, people who are well known to the Minister and recognized by her, are afraid that this temporary, interim measure will become permanent just like income tax.
All last year members of the public tried to meet with the Minister on this matter and could not. The Plaut Report was delayed for six months. It was supposed to be put out in December. The Minister promised it month by month but it did not come out until the middle of June. There was no time for the committee to look at it or deal with it seriously before the summer recess. Members of the public who tried to meet with the Minister and who invited her to their meetings were frozen out. They are now uneasy.
Representatives of those groups are meeting tomorrow in Montreal. They have invited the Minister to attend the meeting and she has assured them that she will. I think it will be a very important and fruitful meeting provided the Minister does not go to it with a take-it-or-leave-it, confrontational attitude, the attitude in which the Bill was presented to us in June. In fact, many representatives of these non-governmental organizations urged that this Bill not be introduced this week but that we wait a few days until the Minister had met with those people who have expertise on this matter to hear their views and have some give and take. Then we would be able to work on this Bill. However, for whatever reason, the Cabinet decision was to charge ahead with the Bill, public be damned.
There has been a reference to conversations held between the Minister, the critic of the Liberal Party and the critic of New Democratic Party. There was a meeting of some one and a half to two hours at which the Liberal critic and I urged the Minister to respect what the public was saying in this matter. We were totally unsuccessful. He simply wanted to move ahead. Of course, he has the votes and, if he moves ahead, then that is the way it will be. However, that will not win the co-operation of the public, which the Minister from time to time says is essential in order to get the job done properly.

What I wish to do is to propose three processes by which we might try to resolve the matter, in spite of the awkward way the present Cabinet and the previous Cabinet have handled it up to this point. First, there is the meeting to be held in Montreal tomorrow. Second, there are amendments to which the Minister has made unclear references. Third, there is the report of our committee to which the Chairman has referred.
With respect to the first point, I hope the Minister will attend the meeting tomorrow with the expectation of a genuine exchange of views. She has a great deal going for her. Many people respect her mightily for the fact that last January she corrected a longstanding inhumanity in the regulations so that the spouse of a Canadian who should be landed, according to law, can now be landed without having to return home for a year and, in effect, break up a family. We welcomed the Minister's action in January.
Then there is the committee's report with respect to detentions, which has not yet worked. The staff is still playing silly games at the Montreal Detention Centre. However, we hope that with the Minister's help, the report on the immigration detention centres will have the positive effect which many people in the non-governmental organizations have worked for.
The second point is with the matter of the willingness of the Minister of Employment and Immigration to consider some amendments. I hope that when we discuss these matters tomorrow the distrust will become less and we can move ahead with a sense of co-operation.
With respect to the amendments, the Minister has said, "we will encourage the adoption of an amendment in committee in this regard", that is say, to maintain a panel of three rather than a panel of one. I wish that he had said that the Government will propose such an amendment. We all know it cannot pass until the Government supports it. When he says that we will encourage it, I am not quite sure what he means. However, I would like it to be made quite clear that there will be a quorum of three for all classes.
The Minister has also referred to a two-year term. He said, "It may be important to accept an amendment regarding the length of time Members will serve in order to indicate that this is clearly an emergency reaction to a specific situation". When the Minister says it may be, that is true, it may be and it may not. However, there is no assurance in that regard. I am glad he is thinking about it. I would like to see an assurance in committee, that is, a motion put forward by the Government.
We should also return to the originally proposed size, that is, limit the members to between 30 and 35 altogether for the sake of dealing with the present backlog, especially the backlog of sponsorship cases. If we go to 50 members, then it will be assumed that the Immigration Appeal Board is the instrument for dealing with refugee hearings. That is what Rabbi Plaut's Report opposes, as does the Chairman of the committee and both opposition critics.
I hope the Minister will take this simple action to make it clear that she is not going to let anyone smuggle in a refugee

determination process under the name of the Immigration Appeal Board.
With respect to the committee bringing its report to the Minister by the end of October as we had hoped, I hope that the Minister will bring a report to Parliament before she tables legislation and before she burns her bridges behind her. She is a proud woman who does not like to change her mind. I hope she will bring a report to Parliament in which she will propose legislation to do this and this and this. In this way time can be put aside for discussion in Parliament and by the public. A result will be reached faster in this way rather than by her using her ministerial power to say definitely: "This is how it will be." If she were to say that, the rest of us would have to figure out how to mobilize to make the corrections that we see are needed to be made. speechtext: Questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Kindy).

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the words of the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap). He was quite positive with respect to some of his recommendations. I would like to ask him to elaborate on how he would solve the refugee problem. Has he any specific ideas which could be incorporated in future legislation in order that we do not have to face this problem again in a couple of years?

Mr. Speaker, I will not go into that issue at length now. The Hon. Member's question is one which is certainly in the minds of many thousands of interested people across the country. I think Rabbi Plaut's Report should be seriously considered. I am not saying that we should necessarily agree with every page of it. However, he does make two worth-while points. The first is that we should have a refugee determination board separate from the Immigration Appeal Board. This is a point about which the Chairman says we should make a clear-cut distinction. It should be made clear that a person who comes here as a refugee, or is asking to be considered as a refugee, has to have the human rights question examined first before we put him through the mill with respect to accepting him as a potential immigrant or a potential deportee. This is a point which was asked to be implemented in principle about eight years ago by a number of interested people. However, it was ignored at the time. Our experience now shows that it would have saved millions of dollars and a great deal of hardship if it had been followed. I hope we will follow it now.
Second, there are many among this 13,000 or 14,000 for whom oral hearings have been called by the Supreme Court if they want them. These cases could be handled outside the refugee process. People who come from certain countries could be advised that under our policy we do not forcibly return people to those countries because of the conditions there. They sometimes do not meet the precise definition of refugee, but we will not force them to return home. In other words, we will
allow them to stay here in Canada unless they find another country which works out better for them. Many people who are in the refugee stream now should not be there. I say that, not because they do not have a good claim, but because their problem could be more readily dealt with by other programs. Why this has never been followed by our enforcement staff is something we may never find out now that the Executive Director of the commission has moved on to other matters. I hope we will at least see some change of attitude now.
Mr. Speaker, I have just a couple of words concerning Bill C-55. Just to put the question in focus-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: How many immigrants did you have in your riding last year?

The hon. gentleman opposite asks how many immigrants I had in my riding last year. I can honestly tell him that I have received a couple of requests with which 1 am dealing.
Since there is a need to say a few words to set this particular debate in its true light, it is for that purpose that I rise today. Number one, Mr. Speaker, speaking personally, I cannot see anything that is wrong in this Bill. I think that is probably the first time I have ever said that. Having said that, I must say that I cannot see any great advantage either.
We have a situation in Canada today, I think Hon. Members will agree, where there are about 1500 cases of family sponsorship applications in the works, give or take 100, and
15.000	cases of refugees appearing before the Board, give or take 5,000. Fifteen thousand cases would probably cover
20.000	people before the Board. By increasing the size of the Board from 18 to 50 and carrying out various changes, perhaps an extra 100 cases per year could be processed. It will not do any harm to make that increase, but when one looks at the magnitude of the problem one asks the question: when is the Government going to address the real problem? That is the question.
When did the problem arise? It did not arise last year or the year before or the year before that. This particular problem of blocking the system arose in the past less than a year ago, and the reason for it is this.

speechtext: A few words, George.

Yes, a few words. Why do we have this clogging? When one looks at the appeals under the family sponsorship appeal program, that is not a cumbersome appeal, that can be dealt with very quickly. Member from Calgary asked the question, "How can you solve the refugee problem"? As the Hon. Member knows, the previous system was that when the refugee put in his claim he was interviewed

by a representative of the advisory committee. It was a written representation. At no time after that was that person able to appear in person.
So the decision of the judge was perfectly understandable in that particular case. That has clogged the system. What happened then? The system is clogged in any country which is a signatory to a United Nations Charter which agrees to accept refugees because, as the Hon. Member pointed out a few moments ago, the applications for refugee status are before the same board as are the applications for family sponsorship appeals.
So we are left with this incredible problem that happened only recently, since this Government came to power. What we are saying is that this Government has to try to solve that problem immediately. I am not a member of the committee that visited the detention centres.
That is why you don't know what you are talking about.

If the hon. gentleman listens he is going to learn something. The detention centres were never intended to house the people that are there. They were meant for detention centres. The system was clogged, and therefore that created additional problems. If Members of Parliament would look at the system they would find it to be rather interesting. When landed refugees arrive in, say, Toronto or in Vancouver or some other province, if they do not stay at a detention centre and if an organization will not take them in then they are not entitled, in most provinces, to social assistance. But in other provinces they are, in Quebec they are and in Newfoundland they are. If they get off a plane in Newfoundland and ask for refugee status they are taken care of immediately by the social asssistance department. They qualify to be housed, to eat and to have clothing. But in other provinces they do not qualify for that similar assistance.
The fact of the matter is that this whole thing should be looked at in some detail by the Government, and I am surprised that the Government has not addressed the problem. I think the problem has arisen in this Chamber with the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party saying on this particular Bill, "Now just hold on a minute". There is nothing in it that does any harm but it is not solving the problem and there are so many problems that need to be solved. If the Minister had said, "Look, this is not really going to solve any problems but we are going to process an extra 100 a year" there would not be, I think, the division today. But the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) said in Vancouver, as we will all recall, Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) said that one of our responses to the problems of those seeking refugee status in Canada is Bill C-55. When that happened all of the groups across this country that were concerned about this question were in a virtual uproar and the opposition Parties in the House were then saying, "If this is the response of the Government we are not going to accept it because it is not a good enough response."

Mr. Speaker, having set the record straight and having informed Members of what is really before this Chamber today and why the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party have taken the position they have, 1 will take my seat and await any questions that the hon. gentlemen might wish to ask.

Mr. Speaker, I said I was not going to take part in the debate, but since yesterday, I have been listening to Hon. Members talk about immigration, and I think they need a course on the subject, especially the previous speaker. I was taking some notes while he was speaking, and 1 would like to ask him a question. The Bill before the House today would increase the number from 18 to 50. Mathematically speaking, he said it would mean only 100 more cases, but 1 think that, considering the humanitarian aspect, 100 people are worth more than his own attitude to the subject.
Earlier, the Hon. Member said he had seen a few claims by people who had requested immigrant status in his riding. In my riding we have 275 claims pending. Thirty-three per cent of the population consists of new Canadians. There are people who have been in this country for five or six years and who are still waiting to receive employment permits and refugee or immigrant status. This is certainly not the fault of the present Conservative Government, but the Government to which the Hon. Member belonged when it was in power, and which did nothing. Today, we simply want to increase the number so that we can at least admit from 100 to 125 more people and activate the system, pending a complete reform of the legislation on immigration and refugees. Just now, the Hon. Member mixed up refugees and immigrants when he was talking about detention.
When a refugee arrives at a Quebec port of entry and asks for political asylum he is put in a detention camp. It is a prison, my friend, when you consider that the man is locked up in a 7-by-7- or 10-by-12-foot room where he cannot even see daylight. It is particularly bad for someone from another country who was badly treated, both physically and mentally, and gets that kind of reception in Canada. This has always been the Liberal Party approach: Come in, my friend, and we will throw you in jail! That is called detention, Sir.
I think that the Bill should be adopted. I sit on the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration where we debated the issue of refugees and immigrants on at least forty different occasions and, believe me, it is about time we took some action. It is better to take half a step than to stand still as they have done for the past 15 years.

Mr. Speaker, I must admit the hon. gentleman is a member of the committee and perhaps he believes he knows more about the subject than I do. However, let me point

out where he is a little bit off track. The system became clogged because, although the Immigration Appeal Board deals with those cases he mentioned of family sponsorship, it also deals with people seeking refugee status. That is a complicated procedure compared to the first group, and the IAB should not be dealing with the refugee question. We are saying this because this problem has become so serious that there should be another mechanism in place to deal with it.
