speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Layton (for the Minister of Agriculture) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-42, an Act to dissolve Canagrex and to amend certain Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise on second reading of Bill C-42 which is designed to repeal the Canagrex Act and hence dissolve this Crown corporation.
Hear, hear!
A great day for Canada.

As the House is aware, in November, 1984, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced a number of initiatives aimed at reducing Government expenditures. One
such initiative involved the decision to phase out Canagrex by April, 1985. This has been done. This Bill is intended to repeal the Canagrex Act and hence formally dissolve this Crown corporation.
It is a short Bill containing seven clauses. Its major feature, Clause 4, provides for all rights, property, obligations and liabilities of Canagrex to be the rights, property, obligations and liabilities of Her Majesty. For example, the contingent liability respecting the loan for sales to Cuba incurred by Canagrex is transformed into a liability of Her Majesty. Subclause 4(3) provides the specific authority for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to do all that is required in the winding up of the corporation. Section 100 of the Financial Administration Act provides that a Crown corporation may not be dissolved unless authorized by Parliament. The Canagrex Dissolution Act is meant to be such an authority.
Members will be pleased to know that positions were found or settlements made for all of the 30 staff of Canagrex, either in the public or the private sector. All operational files were turned over to the Department of Agriculture and measures have been taken by that Department, the Department of External Affairs and the Export Development Corporation to facilitate additional agricultural and food exports by the private sector.
As the Minister explained to the Standing Committee on Agriculture on December 18, 1984, it was obvious to all that Canagrex had start-up problems. While it undoubtedly would over time, have increased the volume of exports assisted, it was clear that Canagrex was not going to achieve the targets originally expected, nor was it going to be utilized by industry as planned. The activities provided for in the Canagrex Act were market identification and promotion, export counselling, provision of grants and contributions, state to state trading, loans and guarantees, the ability upon request to enter into joint ventures, and the power to import, export and buy and sell. Market identification missions, intelligence and analyses can and are being undertaken by both Agriculture Canada and External Affairs, as are market promotion activities, seminars and trade fairs. State to state trading, buying and selling and exporting may, if necessary, be undertaken through the Agricultural Products Board legislation. Grants and contributions are provided for under the PEMD food program of External Affairs. Insurance, loans and guarantees are available from the Export Development Corporation. Their services to the industry are in the process of being expanded. Cana-grex's export counselling and co-ordinating role will be undertaken by Agriculture Canada.
On March 1 1, 1985, Mr. Story, the President of Canagrex, appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture. In answer to a question as to who should co-ordinate and follow up the work started by Canagrex, he indicated his personal view that it should be Agriculture Canada. On June 20, 1985, the audit committee of the Board of Directors of Canagrex had a board meeting by way of a conference call in which a member of the Auditor General's office participated, and the report to the Minister on the financial statements of Canagrex
September 27, 1985

for the year ending March 31, 1985, was agreed to. These accounts indicated that for the year and Canagrex had a surplus of $1,846,278. Guarantees outstanding under the Cuban line of credit amounted to $8,311,728 as at March 31, 1985. These guarantees are to be assumed by the Department of Agriculture when the corporation is dissolved pursuant to Bill C-42. It should be noted that these guarantees will expire as of December 9, 1985. When proclaimed, Bill C-42 will result in the orderly liquidation of the corporation.
Canada's current financial situation demands action. The question was where within the agricultural portfolio cuts could be made that would be the least painful in both human and program impact. Canagrex fit such criteria. While painful, it is believed that the end result will be a streamlining and rationalization of agricultural and food exporting activities of the federal Government. The decision to wind up Canagrex was taken after a careful weighing of the factors involved and the impact such a decision would have on the agri-food sector. It should be stressed that the facilitating of additional exports of agricultural and food products continues to be a top priority of the Government. I believe that with the full co-operation of all federal Departments and agencies involved in facilitating export marketing, the private sector will be able to expand its exports on a more cost-effective basis.
I believe, as I know my colleague, the Minister of Agriculture does, that Bill C-42 is sound, desirable, and in the interests of Canadian agriculture and I urge Members on all sides of the House to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few words to say on Bill C-42, an Act to dissolve Canagrex. This Bill is designed to wind up this Crown corporation, although it was effectively destroyed last November 8 on "Black Thursday" when the Government cut its financing including $60 million in cuts from agriculture. That was just the beginning of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) taking on the responsibility of presiding over the decline and destruction of the federal Department of Agriculture. It is interesting that while our agricultural industry is facing its most difficult time in the history of the country since the 1930s, we are spending our time dissolving an agency which was established by the Parliament of Canada to promote, develop, and enhance our trading in agricultural commodities around the world with all the flexibility of a Crown corporation. Rather than trying to solve the tremendous problems facing agriculture, we are debating a Bill which will destroy a very fundamental instrument for the development and promotion of agriculture.
During the election campaign the Government talked about enhancing trade, but in the election manifesto which was put out in Prince Albert it was never mentioned that Canagrex would be wound up. There is a whole raft of issues that have been set on the shelf for months with no decisions being made. The Minister of Agriculture put a moratorium on farm bankruptcy foreclosures last fall. All through the winter and spring months we were promised that there would be something in
Canagrex Dissolution Act
the Budget to deal with the terrible farm financial crisis which is faced by approximately 39,000 farmers in the country. There was provision in the Budget to assist farmers to get out of agriculture, but nothing to help young farmers stay in the business. The 39,000 farmers who are in serious financial difficulties today are our youngest, most technologically advanced, and most productive farmers. Those farmers produce half of the food in this country, but nothing was done for them in the Budget or in the Estimates of the Department of Agriculture. It is really said that rather than debating a Bill to provide enhanced funding to solve the serious financial difficulties, as was recommended and supported by the Conservative caucus Members, we are debating a Bill to destroy one of the agencies which was established by the Parliament of Canada to enhance our trading relationships in the country.
It is interesting that within a matter of three or four weeks of taking office the new Liberal Government in Ontario announced a $50 million program for assistance for farmers facing serious financial difficulties. The federal Government has been in power for over a year and it has been unable to effect a rescue operation to assist agriculture. When one considers the lack of action by the Government one must wonder whether the Government is determined to have a shakedown. It is saying that its policy is that of the survival of the fittest-if these guys can make it on their own, that is great, but if they cannot, that is acceptable.
In the documents that the Government is using in trading with the United States we see that the Government is considering leaving farm stabilization programs and marketing systems in the negotiations. If those marketing systems are thrown on the bargaining table in Washington, I predict that rather than having 23 per cent of our farmers in serious financial difficulty there will be 33 per cent in that situation, as there are in the United States.
I read with great interest the papers which the Minister of Agriculture put on the table at the meeting in St. John's, Newfoundland, in July. He said that the Government would move toward a free market economy in farm commodities.
Hear, hear!

I hear the Hon. Member opposite saying "Hear, hear". Does he believe that the United States system of marketing farm commodities or the European Economic Community system of marketing farm commodities is better than the controlled commodities in this country?
This week in the United States there is a conference taking place between the Senate and the House of Representatives to decide whether assistance for farm support and subsidy programs should be $45 billion. Clearly, Washington and other capitals of Europe such as Paris, London and Bonn are much more wealthy central governments than in Canada. If we are going to throw our marketing system and stabilization programs on the table for the free trade negotiations, I do not

September 27, 1985
Canagrex Dissolution Act
believe that Canadian farmers will come out very well in that arrangement.
Clearly, the Government documents indicate that that is exactly what it is contemplating. I ask the Hon. Member opposite where he thinks agriculture in western Canada would be today if it was not for the crop insurance program and the western grain stabilization programs which have paid out approximately $1 billion in the last 12 months? We should be debating programs to try to solve the serious financial difficulties facing Canadian farmers today rather than this Bill which winds up Canagrex-an organization which could have promoted and increased our exports in a long list of commodities through assistance in financing, market promotion, insurance and in developing and analysing markets. However, we are debating a Bill to destroy Canagrex rather than addressing other serious problems facing Canadian agriculture.
During the committee meetings the Hon. Minister of Agriculture who I understand has a large farming section in his riding, quoted Mr. Story, President of Canagrex. When Mr. Story appeared before the Agriculture Committee last winter, he described a phone call that he received on the night of November 7, 1984, when the Minister phoned and said that the next day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) would be destroying Canagrex by removing all of its funding. Mr. Story responded that he was sorry. If one checks the minutes of the committee meeting, the Minister responded that he was also sorry and, of course, this demonstrates the tremendous split in the Tory caucus over the Canagrex Bill. Clearly there was great support from Members like the Minister of Agriculture while others in the Tory caucus from other parts of the country were very much opposed to it.
This Bill to destroy Canagrex will destroy a Crown corporation that was designed to assist in market identification, the penetration of new markets, the expansion of existing markets and the identification of foreign competition. Canagrex had moved effectively in these areas by having trade missions in many countries identifying markets and starting markets analysis in those smaller commodities produced by less organized groups that do not come under the Canadian Wheat Board or the Canadian Dairy Commission. 1 do not believe that the Department of Agriculture or the Department of External Affairs have the capacity to do that job nearly as well.
Canagrex also worked in promotion asisstance for trade missions, fairs and exhibitions and helped in product development and advertising programs. This is one of the most aggressive times in our history, when every country in the world is fighting for agricultural markets. Practically every country in the world has massive programs to obtain these markets. The United States agricultural food program is a massive program to do those things that Canagrex was designed to do. SOPEXA is the program in France to promote market development and the sale of farm commoditites. Valery Giscard d'Estaing, the President of France, described it as the nation's green oil because no organization, apart from that in the United States, has conducted the kind of aggressive sales, promotion and development that the EEC has done.
Let us consider the EEC. A few years ago it was purchasing approximately 25 million tonnes of grain. Now it is marketing massive amounts of grain throughout the world. The Federal Republic of Germany has its CMA organization. Isreal has its own agricultural promotion and export institute. Mexico has its national company for popular subsistency. Greece has a market promotion program as well.
We are dealing in a very competitive world. We have active promotion of commodities controlled by the Canadian Wheat Board and the Canadian Dairy Commission. However, Canagrex was designed to assist in those other commodities not covered by those commissions. Canagrex would have provided transportation services, information assistance, insurance advice, regulatory advice, estimates and other services in order to assist smaller groups such as co-ops. Canagrex was designed to provide financial assistance, loan guarantees, loan financing, grants and contributions.
It would have assisted service related activities, the transfer of technology, consulting and management activities as well as joint ventures. This was a Crown corporation designed to assist the smaller commodity groups in marketing their products abroad. I believe that the Government is making a mistake by winding up this Crown corporation because it provided a valuable contribution to the agricultural community in this country. Let us look at some of the items and areas of the world where Canagrex was just starting to develop systems and programs. For instance, dairy cattle going to Latin America, Southeast Asia and North Africa. Many of these countries trade state to state. It is a big advantage to have a corporation like Canagrex. We are talking about dozens of millions of dollars providing financial assistance, technical assistance, insurance and promotion.
Look at the opportunities for selling semen to countries in North Africa, a state to state business, estimated at $14 million. Look at selling our Holstein-Friesian dairy cattle to countries in eastern Europe by joint ventures. The estimate was $40 million over the next 10 years for sales of breeding stock.
If we look at the opportunities for breeding swine in Southeast Asia on a joint venture possibility, some $5 million a year was the estimate. What about feed grains to areas in Africa in a joint venture partnership? What about canola going to Latin America, another joint venture? That was estimated at $50 million in the short therm and up to $150 million over the long term.
We are dealing here with an agency that had the flexibility of a Crown corporation. Our Conservative friends have shown us that they are very supportive of some Crown corporations. Look at Petro-Canada. A takeover of an American corporation, Gulf Oil has just been approved at a cost of $900 million. Canagrex is a very small Crown corporation which was serving agriculture, especially commodities that are not supported by massive marketing agencies. The assistance that Canagrex could give in co-ordinating some of Canada's activities is
September 27, 1985

important. Now we have groups going from Ontario, Alberta and other provinces, marketing commodities and livestock in other parts of the world in competition. Canagrex was to be an agency which could have assisted and helped all Canada's provinces, whether big provinces with nine million people, such as Ontario, or whether a small province, such as Prince Edward Island with only 130,000 people.
We see an action here today, the destruction of a Crown corporation, which could have benefited the country.
Let us have some more.

At the same time we hear the Tories cheering on the destruction of this Crown corporation, we do not hear any word of the drought program, which is needed in western Canada for the grain sector. This program has been promised week after week. I believe three weeks ago the Minister said that in a couple of weeks he would be announcing drought assistance to those areas affected in western Canada. The decision to support the Canadian Commercial Bank was made over a weekend, perhaps made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) alone who passed on the word to the Finance Department and then on to the two Ministers of Finance. This decision involved a billion dollars. Yet it has taken weeks and weeks to come up with any assistance for the drought problem in western Canada.
We have been waiting for months for the Government to act on its new dairy policy. The Minister promised faithfully a year ago that he would have a dairy policy in place by August of this year. It was not until about July 14 that he got around to appointing a couple of representatives to analyse the situation and recommend a dairy policy.
I mentioned earlier that there had been no action in the Budget or in the Estimates on the farm debt crisis. Likewise, there has really been no decision on farm debt legislation relating to foreclosures, specifically a preforeclosure arbitration procedure. The Minister announced on July 10 that legislation would be brought in this fall. He said if the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) did not bring in legislation concerning the Bankruptcy Act, then he would bring in amendments to the existing Bankruptcy Act.
When my motion on that subject was debated a couple of weeks ago, we got a very equivocal statement by the Parliamentary Secretary, who speaks on behalf of the Government in matters of agriculture.
Is the Government supporting that concept or not, which the Minister clearly enunciated in early July? In any event, he said it was all up to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
There is a need for this type of legislation, which was shown in the Grey-Bruce pilot project report. There was a Bill before the House in June, 1984. That is 15 or 16 months ago. All the Government had to do was to reintroduce that legislation, but nothing has happened in the last 14 or 15 months to indicate exactly where the Government is going.

Daily we have the banks turning down the screws on farmers who are losing their farms. The Minister indicated that there were 675 farms waiting to be foreclosed by the FCC at the time he placed a moratorium on that. He has not indicated what he plans to do with regard to the foreclosures in the private sector, if anything at all.
It was not just a $60 million cut-back last November 8 that the Agriculture Department underwent, which snuffed out the life of Canagrex. In the Estimates the Government says it is going to cut back another $50 million, but it is not clear where. Is it in research which would be sort of cutting off the future? Is it in transportation assistance for farm commodities? Is it in the stabilization payments, meaning inadequate assistance for the farm drought plague in western Canada? Is it in the dairy support program?
There is another little hooker in the Budget, which most people missed, about which we made inquiries. We have made inquiries about the budget of the Department of Agriculture being deindexed. Not only will there be a $50 million cut-back every year for the next four years or five years, but with the deindexation of its budget there will be a $10 million or $15 million reduction in its purchasing power. Not only in Canagrex being cut by the Government. The entire Department of Agriculture is being de-emphasized at a time when the agricultural community is experiencing a devaluation of farmlands and a continuing low level of farm commodity prices. This situation is being exacerbated by the programs of other countries such as the United States and those in the European Economic Community.
Last year the Government made a commitment in the election campaign to do away with the farm fuel excise tax. It did away with that tax and gave a rebate on the petroleum compensation charge. The two together amounted to some 3 cents per litre on the excise tax and 1.8 cents per litre on the petroleum compensation charge. Lo and behold, when the petroleum compensation charge was done away with on June 1, the price of gasoline did not drop. It may have even risen because of deregulation. However, the exemption of 1.8 cents per litre or 7 cents per gallon disappeared for farmers. If we look at the Budget, we see that the Minister imposed a fuel tax on all Canadians but provided no exemption for primary producers in the forestry, mining, fishing or farming community.
On September 3, we saw the introduction of what has come to be known in western Canada as a harvest tax of 2 cents per litre or 9 cents per gallon. That was imposed in less than a year, by a day, from the time the Government was elected. It was another promise forgone. During the period from June 1 to September 3, if we total the excise tax and the petroleum compensation exemption, we see a total increase of 16 cents per gallon for farmers. At the same time the Minister of Finance imposed that excise tax, he also imposed a 1-cent tax on ail farm input commodities, which will involve another $11 million for 1986.

When the Government finally decided to relent and not to deindex old age pensions, it imposed another 1-cent per litre or 4.5 cents per gallon, effective on January 1, 1987, on fuels for farmers and other primary producers. The Minister of Finance has steadfastly denied that he will give an exemption to farmers. At the same time that 1-cent per litre or 4.5 cents per gallon comes into effect, the exemption of 3 cents per litre provided by the Minister last September will come off. Therefore, from the period of June 1 to a year from December 31, we will see a dramatic increase which will be far greater than that of last year. We should not be winding up Canagrex. The Minister said to the President of Canagrex he was sorry that the Government was taking this action when he informed him of it last week. Various federations of agriculture and the National Farmers Union have supported Canagrex, as well as small commodity groups which are not large enough or strong enough to compete in the area of international sales. They are the ones who will be hurt by the winding up of Canagrex. They will be unable to compete with the marketing agencies of various countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom, France and those in the EEC. The dissolution of Canagrex is a backward step. I hope the Government will reconsider its action, especially at a time when agriculture faces one of its most difficult times in history.
Just a few weeks ago, in the last week of August, the Bruce County Federation of Agriculture, a responsible group, passed a resolution at a meeting in Chesley. Some 200 to 300 farmers supported this resolution which called for a total moratorium on farm foreclosures. Surely this is the kind of problem we in the House of Commons should be addressing. In view of the farm debt crisis, we should be providing financial assistance, not just calling for a moratorium. We should be debating legislation such as that proposed by the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs in its report last March.
The Minister called upon people to make representations on how the Farm Credit Corporation can be improved. Last February and March, some of the members of the Standing Committee on Agriculture served on the Finance Committee of the House of Commons which heard from dozens of groups including the provinces and the federal Departments concerned. They received written submissions and heard representations recommending a program for the 39,000 or 40,000 farmers facing serious financial difficulty. The majority of members on that committee were from the Government side and they said that this was the greatest priority. Approximately 12,000 or 14,000 of those farmers facing financial difficulty should be assisted. Some of them do not require assistance, even though they are in serious financial difficulty, because they have other sources of income and so on; perhaps some are at a point where they cannot be helped. The committee identified perhaps 12,000 to 14,000 that could be helped by a program. The committee was composed of representatives from all sides of the House and recommended a program with
funds of some $96 million to $98 million per year for the next several years to see that this group of young, productive, technologically advanced farmers could remain on the land through low-interest rate loans of approximately 8 per cent. Surely that is the kind of legislation that we should be debating in the House today. We should be trying to find a solution that will solve the problems of today as well as maintain for tomorrow that group of farmers who will lead the agricultural industry in the years ahead and will provide the food that this country and other countries need.
I cannot agree with the decision of the Government to wind up Canagrex as a Crown corporation. I think we should be enhancing our trading relationships and helping the small commodity groups to enhance their operations. We should be giving them the tools that the large commodity operations like dairy and wheat already have, tools which are needed because of today's world situation.

Mr. Speaker, this can be called my Hon. Eugene Whelan memorial speech. The previous Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor was, of course, the architect of Canagrex. It is important to remember that his long and hard fight as Minister of Agriculture to establish this agency was something which was strongly backed by farm organizations across the country and just as strongly opposed by some of the major multinational companies that operate in the grain trade and in other parts of our agricultural commodity exchange system.
Perhaps it is not by chance that the memorial of this new Government to my predecessor is not only his dismissal from a post which he might have well filled but also a demonstration that this Government listens to large-scale corporate sector interests rather than to farm organizations, virtually every one of which has indicated its strong and continuing support for this organization.
Perhaps, with their boundless confidence in my predecessor, these farm organizations took his actions on faith. I have to confess that I have not always been convinced that their faith in my predecessor was entirely well placed. However, with respect to Canagrex, an institution which became a part of our international trade system, my predecessor, Mr. Whelan, deserves great credit. I simply wish that Members of the House of Commons would give him that credit for this initiative. The farmers of Canada certainly wish that this institution would continue. They strongly oppose what the Government is doing.
To talk realistically about Canagrex, we have first to recognize the immense crisis that exists in the farming community in our country. I would estimate that 75 per cent to 80 per cent of Hon. Members of this House represent constituencies which are mainly urban. Their interest in food policy is mainly from a consumer's perspective. In making their interest that of a consumer, they are being shortsighted. I express my appreciation at being able to represent a constituency which includes a significant share of farmers who produce the food we eat. It

has certainly given me some appreciation of the tremendous challenges they face and the tremendous contribution they make to this country. The farmers make their contribution under the most difficult circumstances possible. Frankly, these difficult circumstances have been made more difficult by this Government since September of last year.
I would like to deal with a few pieces of background data if I could, Mr. Speaker. Let me deal first with the debt crisis that faces Canada's farmers. According to Farm Credit Corporation statistics, 18 per cent of Ontario farmers face severe cash flow difficulties. In addition to that, the net worth of farms in Ontario declined by over 14 per cent between 1981 and 1984. 1 would ask Hon. Members if this is not the most devastating indication of the growth of this severe crisis in the farm community. The result of this crisis is that the average Ontario farm, as of 1985, is carrying over $25,000 worth of short-term debts as compared to just $3,000 in 1981. The consequence is a decrease of significant proportion in investment in the farm community in new equipment, livestock and land.
This reality is not simply a statistical one. I have before me letters I have sent to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) on behalf of farmers in my constituency who have faced foreclosure over the past winter. As the debt crisis has tightened, they have eventually had to give in to the pressures that they face.
This crisis has reached such proportions that it affects not only isolated cases. Rather, official bodies have come to recognize just how serious this crisis is. The Minister of Agriculture himself set up a task force to study the farm credit situation. When the task force reported back in May, it endorsed precisely the point which we in the NDP have been emphasizing and that is that it is essential to set up a farm debt relief board which could review and renegotiate debts faced by farmers. After all, Mr. Speaker, we do this for foreign countries like Argentina, Chile or Peru. Surely to God we should be prepared to make that same kind of basic commitment to the farmers of Canada. If there were a situation characterized simply by high debts and if there were some sort of relief emerging in the form of improved prices, then the crisis might be something which farmers could face with optimism. However, the reality is that the price situation is just as critical as the debt situation this year.
In my own county, Essex County, two of the major commodities are soybeans and corn. The current cash price for soybeans is $6.30 per bushel, while the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture and Food estimates that it costs a farmer $7.49 to produce that same bushel. We are talking about a difference between price and basic costs of production of $1.19 per bushel. One does not have to be an economist to realize that means the loss of one's shirt. The same thing is true with respect to corn. The cash price for corn stands at $2.60 per bushel while production costs are estimated at $3.60 per bushel. That compares to prices in the last two years of $4 per

bushel. Thus, it reflects a massive decrease. While there has been some increase in production, which has been at a loss of $1 per bushel, it does not do any good. We have a situation in which debts are high-crippling. We have a situation in which prices are low and falling and the consequence affects farm communities, not just in Ontario, but across the country. We have not had a Farm Aid concert which would have dramatically focused attention on farm prices in this country. It is up to Members of Parliament to try to focus that attention for a Government which farmers in the country do not think is listening.
On September 5, I wrote to the Minister of Agriculture after a series of discussions I had with farmers from across my constituency this summer indicating to him, and I quote:
-my meetings with farmers and farm groups in Essex County have convinced me that the economic problems in the farm community in Southwestern Ontario continue to be extreme. Many farmers are facing extremely heavy debt loads, prices for products this year remain low, and the accumulation of past debt service burdens is making the financial position of many farms more and more desperate. The strongly expressed view of farmers in the County is that the Government budget released in May does not provide the required relief which they anticipated; indeed, most farmers have described that budget to me as a betrayal.
In my view, and the view of many of the farmers that I represent, two broad initiatives are very urgently required at this point. First, it is crucial to explore new initiatives to improve prices for Canadian farmers, so that parity objectives can be achieved. As you know, this subject was referred by the House of Commons to the Agricultural Committee last spring, but no further action has yet been taken to pursue the issue. I believe very strongly that you must provide some leadership on these pricing problems, and yourself urge the Agriculture Committee to undertake immediate hearings across the country to investigate various mechanisms for increasing price levels for farm products in this country. It might even make sense to have a special House of Commons task force on this issue, as has been done with a number of other policy questions.
The second broad issue which I feel is crucial, on the basis of discussions with Essex County farmers, is the establishment of a comprehensive debt review board, able to negotiate between farmers and their creditors, in order to establish new payment schedules and interest relief to ease cash-flow problems for many badly pressured farms.
Farm group leaders in my constituency state flatly that financial pressures are now squeezing even very well managed farms, and that relief is crucial to maintain the viability of those farm enterprises.
I went on in my letter to indicate that I would be very pleased to meet with the Minister to discuss these concerns in more detail. My letter continues:
Farm leaders from my constituency, representing both the Essex County Federation of Agriculture and the National Farmers Union would also be very pleased to participate in a discussion with you. There is a great sense of urgency and concern in Essex County, and we all want to provide as much impetus as possible to any government moves in the directions suggested above.

My fellow members on the joint committee on trade this summer know that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture came to us in Winnipeg and said that it was a mistake to do away with Canagrex, that Canagrex was doing a good job. Economists have an approach to assessing institutions and initiatives called cost-benefit analysis. They look at the costs of an institution and they look at the financial benefits of an institution. Usually if the costs are just a little bit less than the benefits they recommend going ahead.
Let us do that with respect to Canagrex. We can do so with official statistics provided by the Minister of Agriculture himself. The House resumed, from Friday, April 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Jourdenais, that Bill C-221, an Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have the opportunity to discuss Bill C-221 in this House. The Bill contains two proposals that deal with the Unemployment Insurance Act. I would like to discuss the proposal for the UI appeal system.
The Bill requests that we repeal an existing section of the UI Act, Section 103, and replace it with another. To properly understand this section of the Act and the ramifications of its removal, I believe we must first look at the present UI appeal system and agree on the purpose of Section 103, and what would happen if it was changed along the lines suggested in this Bill. The UI appeal system has been a part of the UI Act since its inception in the 1940s. It is a bi-level appeal system. The first level of appeal is the Board of Referees. The Board is composed of a chairperson and at least two members, divided evenly amongst two groups, employers or representatives of employers, and insured persons or representatives of insured persons. The chairpersons of the Board of Referees are appointed by the Governor in Council and the other members are appointed by the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission. Unlike, for example, a provincial Court of Appeal, the Board of Referees is not a permanent body with a fixed number of members, any of whom may at any time be called upon to sit, generally as members of a bench or judges, to hear any case within the jurisdiction of the court. The Board of Referees is constituted afresh, each time an appeal is lodged, from panels of members, one panel for each group of representative members, and a panel of chairpersons. All members of the Board are independent of UI and their decisions are based on the UI Act, regulations and previous jurisprudence of the umpire.
The second level of the UI appeal system is the umpire, who is usually a judge of the Federal Court. The principle of the existence of a second level of appeal is not universally recognized in law. Eminent jurists of both the Anglo-Saxon and civil legal traditions have asserted that the existence of a second level of appeal makes the first level virtually useless. In Canadian law, however, the two-tier appeal is the rule rather than the exception. The existence of the Supreme Court of Canada as a general court of appeal has accustomed Canadians who come before the courts to rely on a second level of appeal which can overrule decisions of their provincial Court of Appeal. The same is also true of administrative tribunals which we, the legislators, frequently endow with at least two, and sometimes more, levels of appeal. This adds to the safeguards flowing from the general power of supervision and review which is invested in the Superior Court of every province and in the Fedreal Court.
The existence of a two-tier appeal system in unemployment insurance cases can be explained easily. The subject matter of these appeals is the administration of a piece of social legislation, the purpose of which is to preserve the economic order by protecting wage-earners and developing a common goal between business and labour. It seemed quite natural to involve representatives of the two groups of society most directly

September 27, 1985
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
affected, employers and workers, with the actions of the administrative authorities.
In order to establish some mechanism to review individual decisions concerning the application of the statute, it seemed necessary to add to these two elements, administrative and representative, a third element, maintaining values which are, properly speaking, legal in nature. Since there was a longstanding belief in Canada that neither law nor justice could exist outside the realm of the ordinary courts, we turn to the judiciary to provide this strictly legal contribution in the form of a second level of review of administrative decision.
The umpire is usually the final level of appeal for litigation regarding unemployment insurance benefits. The impact of the umpire's decisions, however, is not limited to merely settling the cases brought before him. In contrast to the decisions of the Boards of Referees, decisions of the umpire have been regarded as a source of case law ever since the early days of unemployment insurance.
This is how the UI appeal system is set up. How well does it work? Is it really the impartial, just, fair and logical system everyone tells us? If a claimant disagres with a decision on his or her claim, he or she has the right to appeal that decision to a Board of Referees. All claimants are told of this right when they are told of the decision on their claim. All claimants are told that they have 30 days within which to make this appeal. They are told what information should be included in their letter of appeal and where to send it. It is explained to them how their case will be decided by a Board composed of a chairperson and employer and employee representatives, and what they can expect at the hearing itself.
Every effort is made, Mr. Speaker, to make the Board hearing as easy as possible for people to attend. The hearing itself is free. There are many board centres across Canada so they are easily accessible. For claimants in remote areas, the Commission has established telephone hook-ups so claimants can attend their hearing by phone and answer and ask questions of the Board. Each claimant who appeals receives a copy of the file that the Board of Referees has on their case. They get this document before the hearing so that corrections or additions can be made. They are told when and where the hearing is to be and if they cannot attend, it is rescheduled. Every effort is made to have a fair, just and impartial hearing.
What happens if the Board of Referees upholds the Commission's decision? All claimants have the right to appeal to the second level of appeal, the umpire. The appeal must be made within 60 days. Under special circumstances the umpire can extend that limit. All appeals to the umpire must be made on certain grounds which are explained to claimants when and if they lodge an appeal. It is also carefully explained to all claimants that if the decision of the Board of Referees is favourable to them, then the Commission or their employer also have a right to appeal to the umpire. There is also a 60 day time limit in which to lodge this appeal.
Section 103(1) of the UI Act basically says that if a Board of Referee's decision is favourable to a claimant UI pays that claimant whatever is due, even if the Commission is going to
appeal, or does appeal, to the umpire. However, Section 103(2) of the Act goes on to say that if an appeal is lodged within 21 days for either of the following situations, then UI doesn't have to pay the claimant until the umpire has heard the case. The two, and I stress the only two, types of situations when payment can be stopped are where it involves labour disputes or where the Board or Refugees erred in law or did not take into account a provision of the UI Act or regulations.
Naturally, if the umpire rejects the appeal, the benefits that have been withheld are paid. The exception made for appeals involving a labour dispute can be justified by the size of the amounts at stake. Since these are often test appeals, the settlement of which affects an entire group of claimants, large amounts of money are often involved. In those cases where the appeal is based on the allegation that the Board of Referees failed to take into account all relevant provisions of the Act or regulations, the decisions in question are alleged to be manifestly erroneous and it would be an abuse of process to let them take their course. Withholding payments at the instigation of UI is a form of protection for the unemployment insurance amount; in the case of a labour dispute against a decision which, even though it may at first glance seem defensible, entails particularly serious financial consequences for many claims and in the case of an error in law, against a decision which seems indefensible at first glance. If we were to change the existing Section 103 to the one proposed in Bill C-221, a very imaginative and creative Bill, I think the effect would be immediate, and perhaps damaging, to the control of the UI account. The question raised by Bill C-221, what happens if the claimant receives a favourable decision, I believe is a fundamental one.
As I mentioned earlier, the present Section 103(1) states very clearly that if a claimant receives a favorable decision from the Board of Referees, and the area of appeal is not one of those covered by Section 103(2)-labour disputes or an error in law-the claimant is entitled to all benefits payable as a result of that favourable decision. The difference between the present Section and the proposed Section in Bill C-221 is only a few words, but a few words that could cause a difference to the unemployment insurance account.
I believe I can show the House the difference more clearly with the following practical example. A man quits his job and applies for unemployment insurance. He has the necessary weeks of insurable employment and the claim for UI is approved and set up for him. But he quit his job, and after talking to him it is felt that he did not have a good reason for quitting. Consequently, a six-week penalty, called a disqualification, is put on his claim. The man agrees with this decision and does not exercise his right to appeal to the Board of Referees. Ten weeks later, during an interview at the local Canada Unemployment Centre to help him in his search for work, he says that he is tired and plans to take a break and not look for work for a few weeks. He is advised that in order to continue to be eligible for UI he must be available, capable, and actively looking for work each and every day while
September 27, 1985

collecting UI benefits. It is determined that the man has, in fact, stopped looking for work and, consequently, payment of benefits are suspended indefinitely. This decision is felt to be unfair by our hypothetical man and he decides to appeal to the Board of Referees. The Board reviews his case and, for the sake of this example, decides in his favour.
Under the existing Section 103, Mr. Speaker, our man is now entitled to any UI benefits due him since the start of the indefinite suspension. But here is the difference between the present version of Section 103 and that proposed by Bill C-221. Under the Bill C-221 version our man is now entitled to benefits "form the day the initial claim for benefits is made .. ." Since our man also had a six-week disqualification from beneftis for quitting his job, those benefits are now payable too. They are payable under this proposal even though they were not in dispute or even under the Board of Referees' jurisdiction to consider.
The unemployment insurance system has evolved since its inception in the 1940s. It has responded to changing times, but it has never changed without careful examination and longterm study of the effects of these changes. The UI appeal system has changed and evolved over the years too. Section 103 is not there to penalize anyone or any group. It is there to ensure that those people entitled to benefits get them, and that those people not entitled do not.
My hon. colleague's proposal is interesting and comes at an appropriate time. As the House is aware, the Government recently set up a commission of inquiry on unemployment insurance. The commission will be travelling across the country to meet with Canadians to discuss their concerns and listen to their proposals for changes and improvements to the present unemployment insurance program. I think it is fitting to note that the chairman of this commission of inquiry, Mr. Claude Forget, is a distinguished Canadian who has already served the country this year through his expert work with the sub-committee on the revision of the copyright law. Mr. Forget is a former Cabinet Minister in the Liberal Government of the Province of Quebec and his work in social programs is recognized internationally.
I submit that the work of this commission will probe every aspect of unemployment insurance including the actuarial, the financial, the reserve, and the necessity for taxpayers to supplement the system. However, I am told by Mr. Forget that it will also include the humanity of dealing with claimants in unemployment insurance offices. I think that is immensely significant.
I had the opportunity to deal with a constituent in the south side UI office in Edmonton. The Kafkaesque treatment of this claimant, who had been disqualified from benefits because it was suggested that since he was a commission salesman he was not insurable, resulted in this man being reduced to eating one meal a day and truly becoming a hardship case. He was resourceful enough to write an 11-page appeal to Revenue Canada which was assessing his eligibility and he persevered with his claim. If he has not been able to persevere I shudder to think what would have happened to his health, or indeed,
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
his life. I hope that the new commission on UI will deal effectively with the administrative runaround and bureaucratic bungling to which he was subjected.
It has been suggested that perhaps the House should postpone making any changes to the UI program. It has been suggested that we should allow the commission to do the job that we have asked it to do and that when all levels of Canadian society have been polled that will be the time to make the necessary decisions on the direction the UI program will take. Thus, with the greatest regret, I submit that this most creative piece of legislation might be re-examined in the light of what the Forget commission does and that we have an opportunity to examine the Bill sponsored by my hon. friend, the Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) on another occasion.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part today in the debate on Bill C-221 which is introducing two amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.

The amendments are related to two separate articles of the Act. The first amendment is to Section 103 of the Unemployment Insurance Act which deals with the unemployment insurance appeal system, and specifically with the money payable to claimants as a result of an appeal, and the other amendment is to Section 39 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, which gives the authority to pay unemployment insurance benefits to unemployed people who are on training courses. The intention of the amendment in this area is one that I could hardly object to because it concerns education and training, an area in which I have spent many years of my life. In looking at the explanatory notes I see that:
This Bill entitles a person attending a course or program of instruction or training chosen and paid for by him to receive benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, subject to the approval of the Commission.
That preamble pleases those of us who believe that education and training are one of the major components to relieve unemployment in this country.
The Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) introduced this Bill and gave us his reasons for its introduction when he last spoke. He asked us to pass both amendments and has given his arguments. Many Members-probably most Members in the House today-are sympathetic to those views. This afternoon we heard another Member speak to this subject in some detail about these proposed amendments and that as simple as they may seem and as worth while as they may seem, they can introduce complexities to an already complex Act- parts of which I readily admit that neither I nor my constituents understand.
However, by introducing this Bill the Hon. Member has shown his concern for his constituents and, of course, for the many unemployed in Canada's larger constituency. As we

September 27, 1985
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
know, unemployment has been a major concern to many Canadians over the last few years in particular. The Government program that comes to the rescue and serves the unemployed most directly is the unemployment insurance program.
Over the last few years and particularly in the last few months we have heard much discussion on the many aspects of the unemployment insurance program. The variety of comments-indeed on occasion the volume of comments-are an indicator of the complexity of the issue that we face here today in these two amendments. This is a complexity that is recognized by the Government. We also recognize the impact of any change to unemployment insurance on Canadians and Canada. At the moment, unemployment insurance affects and indeed responds to pregnant women, fishermen, workers who have lost their jobs in many areas and workers who are sick. Many millions have been helped over the last few years by this program. As the amendment before us shows, unemployment insurance has helped people who are taking training of various kinds and who wish to re-enter the job market or wish to improve themselves and their job opportunities. However, unemployment insurance is not just another Government program. It is not a grant or a loan program. It is paid for by Canadians through premiums. Employers and workers alike give part of their earnings every working week to the unemployment insurance account.
In 1984, employers and workers together contributed more than $7 billion to that account. That $7 billion was the major share of the almost $10 billion paid out in 1984 to all unemployment insurance claimants. Because of that, changes to this Act cannot be simply a Government decision. Employers and workers across Canada are participants, partners in the unemployment insurance program. As partners, they too have a say. They have some concern about how the program is run. They know what issues they would like to see considered and we cannot make these changes without the significant consultation which is now going on.
There are many significant questions ahead of us in this field. For instance, there is the question of financing, the role of unemployment insurance in labour market adjustment and the very nature of unemployment insurance service to its clients. We heard the previous speaker explain how the program can deny worthy people of an opportunity to participate just because of some of the wording. Each of these issues and indeed many others must be closely examined and decisions taken to determine the future not only of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the programs but on the economic and labour climate of this country.
The Government has taken the initiative to look at the labour market as a whole. The new Canadian Jobs Strategy is a comprehensive plan to help Canadians find longlasting employment. Hundreds of thousands of Canadians will benefit from the Canadian Jobs Strategy which is designed to address specific problems. Federal funds in that strategy are being used to help those Canadians in the greatest need. Yet, while that strategy is being put in place there is still unemployment insurance. One of the major concerns of the Government is to
ensure that unemployment insurance is part of the over-all labour strategy. The two must surely work together. As most Members are aware, the unemployment insurance program is now subject to the review of the Commission of Inquiry on Unemployment Insurance. The hearings and consultations with interested parties in the coming months will form the basis of the commission's report to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) next March. Through these public consultations, the Commission will provide the Government with firm and accurate advice upon which to base proposals for the future of the whole unemployment insurance program.
This process requires time, Mr. Speaker. The Commission of Inquiry must be given every opportunity to do its job thoroughly and to do it right. It was for that reason last May that this Government introduced and passed Bill C-52, which extended the variable entrance requirements for unemployment insurance and froze the premium rate until December, 1986. The objective of that Bill was to maintain stability while the Commission was in progress.
In July, in announcing the members of the Commission of Inquiry, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) highlighted the importance of the Commission's task. He stated:
The questions the review must face are a challenge to all Canadians. The unemployment insurance program must be, and continue to be, a fair and effective investment in people.
The Hon. Member for La Prairie has demonstrated to all of us his belief in that principle. He is concerned that there are people who need our help. I know all of us in this House agree. The Member has done much more by introducing this Bill. He has highlighted the need for the unemployment insurance review and the difficulty the Commission of Inquiry will surely face as it goes about its task.
Unemployment insurance is there to help people who need help. There are questions. What kind of help to they need in today's labour market conditions? Over the last few years, in particular over the last few months, critics and supporters of the unemployment insurance program have suggested many ways. Some have suggested eliminating maternity benefits, making the entrance requirements much stricter or reducing the amount of money paid to claimants. Others have suggested improvements by extending maternity benefits, loosening the entrance requirements and paying out more money. We cannot look at any of these suggestions, even the amendments put forward in this Bill, in isolation. We must know what effect they will have on the rest of the program, and what effect they will have on the labour market.
In the beginning, unemployment insurance was there to help a worker when he lost his job. It was an insurance program. It still is, but it does much more than that now. Maternity benefits, adoption benefits, fishing benefits, illness benefits, special benefits for workers at age 65 are some of the special needs that are filled by the unemployment insurance program.

As we know, unemployment insurance also finances training, job creation and work sharing. There is no simple definition of unemployment insurance today. Is it an insurance program? To some extent yes. Is it a social assistance program? It is certainly there to ensure that Canadians are able to benefit from the safety net we have built.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate my colleague for the work he has performed in the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration to make sure that this Bill would be introduced in the House. Since I agree with my party that the measures provided for in the Bill will correct serious oversights in the present legislation, I do not think that I will speak at any length in support of the Bill, because it was thoroughly discussed and analyzed on April 19 when it was introduced in the House originally.

Indeed, I am sorry to see that although it is only the second time today that this measure has come before the House that significant opposition is being voiced to it. I have to advise the Hon. Member for Guelph (Mr. Winegard) of a trap into which he has fallen, not relating to the content of the Bill, but when given a preformulated speech from the Minister's office, if one starts in French it is necessary to correct the grammar and make sure that one identifies oneself as being of the correct sex. Therefore, it is not right for him to say- [Translation]
"Je suis heureuse, monsieur le President."

I think it will be perceived that what we have here, what in my native country they call a "fit-up", the Government through the Minister's office is attempting to stifle this Bill. I will not be one to co-operate with that, for I perceive that measure which the Bill provides is a common sense one. It would bring our unemployment insurance system much more into line with European systems in providing, through the unemployment
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 insurance system not a meagre insurance against something seen as a casual accident, but a system of helping the unemployed to get back to work.
I think it is well understood in both languages that one has to step back in order to better jump. I think that-

In the context of an unemployment insurance system, the underlying philosophy has to be consistent. It would appear that we have two separate strains of thought warring for the unemployment insurance system and supplying the philosophical basis for it. On the one hand we have, as is evident in many European systems, the belief that unemployment is a period which should be used to re-equip the unemployed individual for his or her re-entry into the workforce. The other philosophy is that unemployment insurance payments should be made to ease the transition of the individual on to the social assistance system or on to welfare. This Party does not subscribe to that philosophy. It is pessimistic, and I hope no Member of the House would subscribe to it.
I am sad to say that the Government has not brought forth progressive measures in unemployment insurance since its election. That is one reason, I regret, that I cannot hold out too much hope for the present measure. We have seen that vacation pay is to be included in the computation of earnings received after the date of unemployment. This will simply encourage employers and employees to get together so that the person who is to be unemployed will take his or her vacation before being laid off. In a sense it is a measure which will not save much for the Government. It will end up being a needless and ineffective provocation.
We have seen the Government table measures to treat severance pay as earned income for the purpose of calculating unemployment insurance entitlement. I do not believe that measure is consistent with the philosophy which I have outlined for re-equipping people to re-enter the labour force as soon as possible. Severance pay, essentially for older workers, is not something to reduce the financial burden on the unemployment insurance system. It is compensation for loss of employment and, particularly in the case of older workers, compensation for forcible eviction from a pension system which many older workers suffer when they are laid off.
The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) spoke eloquently about the inconsistencies regarding relocation benefits under the unemployment insurance system and the way in which make-work programs, unfortunately, often do not apply to those people who most need them. In the context of the present Bill, the anomaly which is being addressed by it is one of the most serious ones in the present unemployment insurance system. We should have a system which not only encourages but supports all those people, who are prepared to further their education and training, to equip them for areas in which there are skill shortages and demand.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by congratulating my hon. friend from Guelph (Mr. Winegard), who spoke earlier, on his efforts to express himself in French. Unlike the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry), we do not demand perfection, we are not such purists, and I would urge my hon. friend from Guelph to persevere and to speak French more often.
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to present my views on Bill C-221. I want to congratulate my hon. friend from La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) on his decision to table in the House a Bill aimed at amending the Unemployment Insurance Act. Thanks to his proposals, we now have a chance to take a closer look at the legislation and its implementation on behalf of Canadians.
Today I shall only be concerned with the proposed amendments to Section 39, which specifies the conditions under which an unemployed worker may draw ordinary unemployment insurance benefits when attending a course of training authorized by the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission.
Mr. Speaker, in this case we are concerned with innovative uses of the Unemployment Insurance fund. Section 39 repeats Section 57(3)(a) of the 1955 Act. In order to assess the repercussions of the proposed amendment to Section 39, I think we should first have a good understanding of what these innovative uses involve.
In the next few minutes I intend to summarize the objectives of Section 39 in its present form and explain how the legislation is applied.
In accordance with the innovative uses of the Unemployment Insurance fund, trainees receiving unemployment insurance benefits may continue to receive them while taking part in programs designed to upgrade their employability. The purpose of Section 39 of the Unemployment Insurance Act is to simplify the income maintenance provisions for claimants attending occupational training courses.
This procedure supports the following objectives:
First, to accelerate re-entry of claimants in the labour market;
Second, to increase training opportunities for claimants;
Third, to harmonize the objectives of the Unemployment Insurance Act and the National Training Act with respect to training opportunities for claimants;
Fourth, to increase the number of manpower training courses offered to unemployed workers, in accordance with labour market demand.
Trainees may get an extension of their unemployment benefit period and continue to receive unemployment insurance payments for the duration of the course, plus three weeks' benefits afterwards while they seek gainful employment.
Additional allowances-for being away from home, for having someone look after dependents, for moving, or for daily commuting-may be paid pursuant to the National Training Act or allocated directly from funds earmarked for the mobility program. Such additional allowances cannot be given to trainees who pay their own tuition fees.
The selection and presentation of trainess are made in the usual way by employment advisers who follow the normal practice for gathering documentation.
Trainess entitled to unemployment insurance benefits lower than the training allowance they would receive otherwise are eligible for benefits equal to the higher training allowance.
To be eligible for benefits pursuant to the terms of Section 39 the trainee must meet the conditions under which he would apply for unemployment insurance benefits. He must also have been selected by an employment advisor to take an approved training course. Trainees attending approved vocational training courses at their own expense are eligible for unemployment insurance benefits, provided the funds appropriated for that purpose are not used up and the courses meet the requirements of the labour market.
Eligible trainees receive unemployment insurance benefits as income support for the duration of their training. The Government assumes part of the costs, while employers and employees pay the balance through their contributions. However the Government pays the full costs during a benefit period extension granted to a trainee to complete a course, and again during the additional three-week maximum extension to seek employment.
Trainees attending courses paid by the Employment and Immigration Commission are registered for training courses in trades of national or regional importance. Provisions have been made for members of target groups. Trainees may also be asked to take a language course if their lack of knowledge of either official language prevents them from securing employment.
Total appropriations allocated for each calendar year under the terms of Section 39 are set by order in council. The maximum unemployment insurance insurable weekly earnings
September 27, 1985

are reviewed every two years. Maximum weekly benefits in 1984 were $255, and they are up to $276 in 1985, an increase of 8.2 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, statistical data provided by the CEIC indicate that roughly 56 per cent of trainees attending courses this year will have been registered under the terms of Section 39.
The average duration of courses should be 16 weeks and total outlays for fiscal year 1984-85 have been estimated at $234 million-a sizeable sum in every respect. Nobody can say we are stingy and, in fact, it should be considered as a sound investment in our own human resources. It is an effective way to prepare the unemployed for labour market re-integration.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell you more about the proposed amendment to Section 39. In its present wording Section 39 deals with steering benefit recipients towards training courses which meet their aspirations and which are likely to help them improve their earning potential and employment opportunities. Trainees are registered for various courses on the basis of labour market standards set under the National Training Act. In concrete terms, when an unemployed individual attends a course the costs are assumed by the CEIC and income support is provided through unemployment insurance benefits.
If a claimant decides to attend a course of his choice at his own expense and asks that benefits continue to be paid to him under Section 39, he must first comply with the requirements of the National Training Program.
It is expected that during 1984-85, some 4,000 trainees taking courses at their own expense will have complied with these requirements, which are basically concerned with the needs of the labour market and not those of the claimant.
There would not be many changes arising from Bill C-221. Instead of being directed to a training course by the Commission, the claimant would simply be authorized to attend a course. There are some similarities between training courses attended by trainees at their own expense and the policy now in effect which allows the proposed procedure.
According to this policy, a claimant may, on certain conditions, attend a training course and receive unemployment insurance benefits under Section 25, provided an employment counsellor certifies he cannot be sent to a course under Section 39, that he cannot find suitable employment within a reason-
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
able length of time, that the proposed course would increase his chances of finding employment and that he would drop the course if he were offered a job. However, adopting this Bill would entail additional costs for benefits. The claimants covered by Section 39 may receive unemployment insurance benefits equal to the training allowance, if the latter is higher than the former. Furthermore, the benefit period may be extended to 104 weeks if the trainee is on a course.
I would like to point out that the proposed wording of Section 39 would no longer exclude the claimant from benefits for a maximum period of three weeks, for failing to take a course according to the Commission's instructions.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to provide some more details on the financial repercussions of the proposed amendment to Section 39. Out of $227 million earmarked for training in 1984 under Section 39, about $45 million, or 20 per cent, was paid out in the form of extended benefits. These benefits would not have been paid if the recipients had not attended the approved training courses. We are in fact talking about a benefit extension. Take the case of someone who is receiving ordinary unemployment insurance benefits and who is eligible for three more weeks of weekly benefits only. An Employment and Immigration Canada counsellor arranges for the recipient to enroll in a training course at a community college. If the course lasts for nine months, the trainee will be eligible to receive unemployment insurance benefits for a period of nine months. If the trainee receives $275 a week, the extension benefits paid out during these nine months would amount to $10,536.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, I want to say that I admire and respect the good intentions of my colleague in proposing this bill. However, during our review of the unemployment insurance system, the proposals made by my hon. friend could be examined more closely. The Inquiry Commission on Unemployment Insurance will be dealing within the next few months with many questions of this type which are related with unemployment insurance.
